# finite-elements.library: ConstantGradientStiffnessEntries

```plato

    // Every stiffness entry of one constant-gradient element, in global
    // degree-of-freedom numbering: each of its nodes against each of its nodes,
    // and within a pair, each displacement component against each. `components`
    // is how many components a node carries — 3 for a solid, 2 for a plane
    // element — and `gradients` is in the same order as `nodes`.
    //
    // The entries are EMITTED, never accumulated. A coordinate list sums the
    // entries naming a position, so the concatenation of every element's entries
    // is already the assembled matrix.
    ConstantGradientStiffnessEntries(nodes: Array<VertexIndex>, gradients: Array<Vector3D>,
        components: Integer, moduli: LameParameters, measure: Number): Array<SparseMatrixEntry>
        => nodes.Count.Range.FlatMap(i =>
            nodes.Count.Range.FlatMap(j =>
                (components * components).MapRange(rs =>
                    SparseMatrixEntry(
                        nodes[i].Value * components + rs / components,
                        nodes[j].Value * components + rs % components,
                        ElasticStiffnessTerm(gradients[i], gradients[j],
                            rs / components, rs % components, moduli, measure)))));

    // The Lame pair of the plane idealization of an isotropic material. Plane
    // strain keeps the three-dimensional first parameter; plane stress replaces
    // it with the reduced value E nu / (1 - nu^2). That single substitution is
    // what makes the plane constitutive matrix identical in FORM to the
    // three-dimensional one, and therefore what lets one stiffness kernel serve
    // both. The shear modulus is the same either way.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_stress)
    PlaneLameParameters(m: EngineeringMaterial, condition: PlaneCondition): LameParameters
        => match (condition)
        {
            PlaneStress => LameParameters(
                Pressure(m.YoungsModulus.Pascals * m.PoissonRatio
                    / (1.0 - m.PoissonRatio.Square)),
                m.ShearModulus);
            PlaneStrain => m.ToLameParameters;
        };

    //==
    // # The linear tetrahedron
    //
    // The constant-strain tetrahedron (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedron):
    // four nodes, linear shape functions, and therefore one constant strain and
    // one constant stress per cell. It is the cheapest usable solid element and
    // the stiffest — a coarse mesh of these under-predicts deflection — but it
    // needs no numerical integration at all, which is exactly what makes it the
    // element to state first.

    // The four vertex indices of a cell, in stored order. (`Vertices` already
    // names this operation for a `TriangleFace` in `meshes.library.plato`; the
    // cell has no counterpart there yet.)
    CellVertices(c: TetrahedronCell): Array<VertexIndex>
        => [c.A, c.B, c.C, c.D];

    // The cell as a standalone solid over a point pool.
    ToTetrahedron(c: TetrahedronCell, positions: Array<Point3D>): Tetrahedron
        => Tetrahedron(positions[c.A.Value], positions[c.B.Value],
            positions[c.C.Value], positions[c.D.Value]);

    // The face as a standalone triangle over a 3D point pool.
    ToTriangle3D(f: TriangleFace, positions: Array<Point3D>): Triangle3D
        => Triangle3D(positions[f.A.Value], positions[f.B.Value], positions[f.C.Value]);

    // The face as a standalone triangle over a plane point pool.
    ToTriangle2D(f: TriangleFace, positions: Array<Point2D>): Triangle2D
        => Triangle2D(positions[f.A.Value], positions[f.B.Value], positions[f.C.Value]);

    // The gradients of the four barycentric shape functions of a linear
    // tetrahedron, in the cell's vertex order. Each is CONSTANT over the cell —
    // that is the entire content of "constant strain": the shape functions are
    // affine, so their gradients, and hence the strain, do not vary inside the
    // element.
    //
    // Gradient i points from the face opposite node i towards node i, with
    // magnitude one over the distance between them. It is built as the cross
    // product spanning that opposite face divided by six times the signed volume,
    // which supplies both the direction and that magnitude at once. Degenerate
    // for a flat cell, whose signed volume is zero.
    ShapeGradients(c: TetrahedronCell, positions: Array<Point3D>): Array<Vector3D>
    {
        var t = c.ToTetrahedron(positions);
        var six = SixTimesSignedVolume(t.A, t.B, t.C, t.D);
        return [
            t.B.Between(t.D).Cross(t.B.Between(t.C)) / six,
            t.A.Between(t.C).Cross(t.A.Between(t.D)) / six,
            t.B.Between(t.A).Cross(t.B.Between(t.D)) / six,
            t.B.Between(t.C).Cross(t.B.Between(t.A)) / six];
    }

    // The 144 stiffness entries of one constant-strain tetrahedron.
    StiffnessEntries(c: TetrahedronCell, positions: Array<Point3D>,
        moduli: LameParameters): Array<SparseMatrixEntry>
        => ConstantGradientStiffnessEntries(c.CellVertices, c.ShapeGradients(positions),
            3, moduli, c.ToTetrahedron(positions).Volume);

    //==
    // # The linear triangle
    //
    // The plane constant-strain triangle: three nodes, two components each, and
    // the same constant-gradient story as the tetrahedron one dimension down.

    // The gradients of the three barycentric shape functions of a linear
    // triangle, in the face's vertex order, as 3D vectors whose Z component is
    // zero.
    //
    // The zero third component is deliberate rather than a lazy lift: it lets the
    // plane element reuse `ElasticStiffnessTerm` unchanged, because every term
    // the third component would contribute is multiplied either by a gradient
    // component that is zero or by a displacement component a plane element does
    // not carry. Degenerate for a collinear face, whose signed area is zero.
    ShapeGradients(f: TriangleFace, positions: Array<Point2D>): Array<Vector3D>
    {
        var t = f.ToTriangle2D(positions);
        var twice = TwiceSignedArea(t.A, t.B, t.C);
        return [
            Vector3D(t.B.Y - t.C.Y, t.C.X - t.B.X, 0.0) / twice,
            Vector3D(t.C.Y - t.A.Y, t.A.X - t.C.X, 0.0) / twice,
            Vector3D(t.A.Y - t.B.Y, t.B.X - t.A.X, 0.0) / twice];
    }

    // The 36 stiffness entries of one plane constant-strain triangle of the given
    // uniform thickness.
    StiffnessEntries(f: TriangleFace, positions: Array<Point2D>, thickness: Length,
        moduli: LameParameters): Array<SparseMatrixEntry>
        => ConstantGradientStiffnessEntries(f.Vertices, f.ShapeGradients(positions),
            2, moduli, f.ToTriangle2D(positions).Area * thickness.Meters);

    //==
    // # Solid analysis
    //
    // Assembling, loading and solving an `ElasticModel3D`. Loads are resolved
    // into `DofLoad` contributions first and summed once at the end, which keeps
    // "which degrees of freedom does this load touch" separate from "add it up"
    // and makes each load kind an independent pure function.

    // Three degrees of freedom per mesh position.
    DofCount(model: ElasticModel3D): Integer
        => model.Mesh.Positions.Count * 3;

    // The assembled global stiffness matrix: every cell's entries concatenated,
    // with no accumulation pass. Independent of the loads and the restraints, so
    // it may be built once and solved repeatedly.
    StiffnessMatrix(model: ElasticModel3D): SparseMatrix
    {
        var moduli = model.Material.ToLameParameters;
        var n = model.DofCount;
        return SparseMatrix(n, n,
            model.Mesh.Cells.FlatMap(c => c.StiffnessEntries(model.Mesh.Positions, moduli)));
    }

    // A concentrated nodal force resolved onto the three degrees of freedom of
    // its node.
    LoadContributions(f: NodalForce3D): Array<DofLoad>
        => [
            DofLoad(DofIndex(f.Node.Value * 3), f.Force.X),
            DofLoad(DofIndex(f.Node.Value * 3 + 1), f.Force.Y),
            DofLoad(DofIndex(f.Node.Value * 3 + 2), f.Force.Z)];
```
